3. Secundò, ens dividitur in ens per se & ens per accidens. Ens
per se, vel metaphysicum, vel physicum, quibus alij addunt artificiale,
morale, & supernaturale. Ens per se metaphysicum, quod aliter di-
citur ens per se simplex, est unica natura, & dicit tantùm unicam en-
titatem partibus prorsus carentem, ut Deus, Angelus, anima rationalis,
& punctum mathematicum : Ens per se physicum est composi-
tum naturale, quod scilicet constat pluribus naturis partialibus na-
turaliter ordinatis ad unum totum constituendum, ut homo, leo,
&c. Ens per se artificiale, dicitur illud quod constat pluribus naturis
totalibus, non ex natura, sed ex arte ordinatis ad unum totum arte-
factum constituendum, ut domus, calceus : Ens per se morale, dicitur
illud quod constat pluribus naturis totalibus, non ex natura aut arte,
sed ex voluntate ordinatis ad unum totum constituendum, ut Res-
publica : Ens per se supernaturale est unicum, scilicet Christus con-
stans ex pluribus naturis totalibus, scilicet Divinitate & humanitate
supernaturaliter ordinatis ad unicam personam aut unum totum per-
sonale constituendum : Cætera entia moralia & artificialia meliùs
revocantur ad entia per accidens. Ens per accidens dicitur illud

page.notes: Marginal notes are fragmentary and split by line-end hyphens; the wording of the notes at "Definitio entis" and "Ens positivum" is partly uncertain, marked [?]. Italic setting is approximate in the definitional phrases. The catchword "Ter-" and the signature "4" are read from the foot of the page; the trailing "4 Ter-" line has been treated as catchword and signature, not as text. The first word "tollit" is a fragment carried over from the previous page. "Cætera" and "Cætera" ligatures are read as æ. Printing errors left as printed, e.g. "sed entia male dividitur" as printed.
